event: On aircraft 376 (used as an XKIT asset), sparks occurred at the main power harness connector when plugging in Havoc battery power on the ground; the fuselage power harness was replaced.
component: AS150 power contact (positive anti-spark contact) on fuselage power harness P/N 107-102189-1
failure_mode: Anti-spark (pre-charge) resistor path in the positive AS150 contact measured about 245 kOhm instead of about 5.6 Ohm, so the connector sparked on mating
contributing: Higher voltage battery bus on the XKIT configuration made the sparking show up
Old harness built before the current AS150 contact QC tests

evidence.quote: duplicate of https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/XKIT-1510 … closing this ticket
Did a resistance check on the positive AS150 terminal of the Fuselage Power Harness, measured ~245 KOhms, should be about 5.6 Ohms.
It looks like a very old harness that pre-dates our new quality control tests for the AS150 contacts.
Performed mating/de-mating of connector with battery ~10 times - no sparks were observed.

team_view_in_comments: Likely, this connector was faulty from the manufacturer and we did not observe sparking until we started using it as an Xkit asset with the higher voltage Battery bus.
reasoning: The VXEP ticket was closed as a duplicate of XKIT-1510. There the positive AS150 terminal of the fuselage power harness measured about 245 kOhm against an expected 5.6 Ohm, which points to the anti-spark resistor path being open. Replacing the harness stopped the sparking over about 10 mating cycles.
notes: Canceled duplicate of XKIT-1510; analysis taken from XKIT-1510. Whether the higher Havoc voltage also contributed was asked in the description but not tested separately.

event: During a preflight motor check on aircraft 481, the VTOL motors could not spin up, made abnormal noises and the HLB percentage swung between 70% and 90%; the center wing and HLB were red tagged and the power connector replaced.
component: AS150 power contact at the 481 center wing HLB connection
failure_mode: Excessive contact resistance (480 uOhm before cleaning, 240 uOhm after, limit 235 uOhm) with heat discoloration, causing a large voltage drop when the lift motors drew current
contributing: Contact may not have been resistance tested at build (records conflict)
Dual current sense assembly also replaced; IBatt1 and IBatt2 readings looked wrong

evidence.quote: AS150 impedance measured 480 uOhms before cleaning, 240 after cleaning. Both fail (limit is 235 uOhms).
4/23/23: Charted Battery current and voltage in correlation to the video. Large voltage drop observed when motors tried to activate.
Also, there is a significant discoloring and indication of heath on the HLB connector, I’m attaching for reference. The battery is located in the battery isolation cabinet.
- Check if 481 contacts were tested previously? Record findings and latest readings in the shared sheet. - measured 163uOhms 11/7. Data in spreadsheet

team_root_cause: 4/23/24: Excessive contact resistance in power connector causing voltage fluctuation.
reasoning: The AS150 contact on the 481 center wing measured 480 uOhm, and still 240 uOhm after cleaning, both above the 235 uOhm limit, and the HLB connector showed heat discoloration. Battery voltage and current charted against the video show a large voltage drop when the motors tried to start. Replacing the power connector resolved the issue.
notes: Records conflict on earlier testing: one comment says the connector was most likely never resistance tested, while the Plan says 163 uOhm was measured on 11/7; the rise from 163 to 480 uOhm suggests degradation, so initiating cause is set to wear_or_age with that doubt. The fault was intermittent: refitting the original HLB did not bring it back. Ticket was canceled for not following process even though the work was completed.

event: On fuel cell aircraft 439, the fuel cell stopped supplying power and stopped communicating with the aircraft early in the flight; the HLB drained and the aircraft returned to base and was recovered undamaged with about 4% HLB.
component: D450XR fuel cell main control board PCA0120 (3V3 rail, U13 BLDC motor driver chip), fuel cell SN D4500252
failure_mode: Internal short of the 3V3 and switched 3V3 rails to ground (cleared by removing U13 and its capacitors), stopping the microcontroller so the fuel cell produced no power and lost its serial link
contributing: No aircraft-side fallback to set fuel cell power when the comm link is lost (VA-1682)
Order of failure (rail surge or chip failure) not known

evidence.quote: Initially probing, the 3V3 and 3V3_SW were shorted together. I removed the P-Channel Mosfet Q3. 3V3 was no longer shorted to GND and only 3V3_SW was shorted to GND. When removing components to find the short, I removed U13 and its coupling capacitors and the 3V3 short was gone.
It was observed that the fuel cell would not power on. No LED activity observed.
All Fuel Cell data stops. What is interesting is that not every variable in the entire log stops. Its why I cant really assess whether the fuel cell isnt performing properly.
replaced main control board (PCA0120)  Performed full calibration sweep of Anode assembly.
Stack health is found to be good. (28.2vdc)

team_root_cause:
Confirmed: PCA0120 (D450XR Main Control Board) Short resulting in failure to output power. Comm link was lost to fuel cell as a result of this failure, requiring return of the fuel cell to validate the failure mode. 
Data review and Physical inspection complete. Result is that PCA0120 Main Control Board for the D450XR had an internal short leading to a failure to produce power. This is the first known instance of this occurrence in aircraft operation. 
“The 3V3 and 3V3_SW were shorted together. I removed the P-Channel Mosfet Q3. 3V3 was no longer shorted to GND and only 3V3_SW was shorted to G
reasoning: Flight data showed all fuel cell data freezing around the start of forward flight while the rest of the aircraft logs continued. On return the fuel cell would not power on, and board-level failure analysis found the 3V3 rails shorted to ground, cleared by removing the U13 BLDC driver chip. With a new PCA0120 the stack tested healthy and the unit passed outgoing QC, which isolates the fault to the control board.
notes: The three RMA-257 QC logs are large post-repair test tables (1.2 to 2.1 MB); I read their headers and scanned them for fault, error and state-change lines and found none, so they only show the repaired unit running. The Plan field mentions PCA0130, but the failed and replaced board is PCA0120 per the failure analysis and RMA-257. The customer mentioned a similar event in battery configuration on the same aircraft; that is VXEP-366, which had a different cause (launch wizard not restarted).

event: On aircraft 459 during automated landing, the vehicle overshot the landing zone by about 1000 ft, hovered back, ignored nudge inputs as expected by the operator, descended onto a wire, and dropped onto the front VTOL boom when motors were cut; the aircraft was replaced.
component: VTOL AP navigation (GPS acceleration correction assumed fixed GPS rate) and fixed-wing helper throttle logic
failure_mode: GPS updates arrived at 4 to 5 Hz instead of the expected 10 Hz and the acceleration correction did not account for the varying dt, giving pitch estimation errors; the fixed-wing helper, driven only by airspeed, added forward throttle while past the touchdown point, making the overshoot worse
contributing: Fixed-wing helper allowed up to 60% throttle
VTOL entry timeout of 30 seconds with airspeed still high
Nudge commands moved target touchdown point without operator feedback
Lift system minimum power fault logged during transition (VT pwr fault: min pwr 0x21)

evidence.quote: @Pat Wells see update above, given we’ve discovered the GPS update rate issue, the inspection of the gyro is not required.  I did confirm in this log that the GPS update rate was 4 or 5hz for most of the flight vs. 10 expected.

Added some notes to this powerpoint - AV459_LandingOvershoot.pptx.  There appears to be an estimation error in pitch that contributes to the overshoot, along with a design/logic bug in the fixed-wing helper implementation.

Fixed-wing helper forward motor throttle command is a function of only the vehicle’s current airspeed.  This works well for a steady hover, but when the vehicle is in transition to VTOL mode it can result in incorrectly increasing throttle when the vehicle is already past the touchdown point and pointed away from it.  Logic should be added to correct this issue.  See https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/VXEP-315 for details.
- Implemented GPS rate calculation in accel updates (this was a separate ticket, but still tested here)

team_root_cause:
- Pitch estimation errors led to the vehicle coming into transition too fast
- Implementation of fixed-wing helper in combination with pitch estimation errors exacerbated landing overshoot.
- Operator nudge commands moved target TDP without providing feedback to the operator.
- Cause of pitch estimation errors unknown.  Current best guess is pitch rate gyro errors.

See report here.

would_settle_it.what: Updated investigation slides tying the 4 to 5 Hz GPS rate to the pitch estimation error in this flight

attachments_read: 21506_RMA Repair Quote for AC VXE-459 Warranty MARSOC 7-1-2024.pdf.md
21983_Sales Order J101687 RMA 240605 Job no. P20070.pdf.md
reasoning: Log review showed the vehicle entered transition too fast because of a pitch estimation error, and the fixed-wing helper then added throttle while past the touchdown point. A later update in the Plan and comments traced the pitch error to the u-blox GPS running at 4 to 5 Hz instead of 10 Hz, confirmed in this log, which dropped the gyro theory; the fix computes the GPS rate in the acceleration updates. This names the mechanism more specifically than the Root Cause field, which still gives the pitch rate gyro as best guess.
notes: The Root Cause field still says the cause of the pitch errors is unknown (best guess gyro), but the Plan field update (6/17) and comment say the GPS update rate issue replaced that theory; I follow the later text. The link from the GPS rate to the pitch error rests on engineering statements and the shipped fix, not on a plotted comparison in the export. An early comment also logged a lift system minimum power fault and climb abort; its role was not investigated further. Aircraft damage per RMA-256: full replacement.

event: Aircraft 439 and other customer aircraft repeatedly failed preflight with the warning that one or more VTOL sensors had failed, blocking launches for about two weeks; no flight took place on the failed attempts.
component: FWAP IMU (includes magnetometer) preflight error checks
failure_mode: FWAP IMU error checks failed in preflight, cause not identified (local magnetic disturbance suspected)
contributing: Possible local magnetic disturbance at the operating site
Generic GCS warning text does not say which sensor failed

evidence.quote: @Pat Wells The error is that the FW AP IMU error checks failed in this case. That IMU includes a magnetometer.  Given that it seems to be failing across a range of aircraft I suspect that there could be an environmental issue. Perhaps local magnetic disturbances, rebar in a reinforced concrete structure is often overlooked.

We have been fighting this for the past two weeks and have only been able to get 5 flights in as this error is constantly repeating.  We have tried separate aircraft, separate GCS, power cycles and Mag Checks and the error is still occurring as of today.
A good number of the messages are generated in the GCS when the vehicle reports that something has failed, but does not say specifically what failed.

team_root_cause: Believed to be an operating procedure that needs to be updated to include restarting the wizard
disagreement: The Root Cause field blames a procedure (not restarting the wizard), but nothing in the ticket shows a wizard restart clears the fault. The customer reports "We have tried separate aircraft, separate GCS, power cycles and Mag Checks and the error is still occurring", and the only engineering review says "the FW AP IMU error checks failed", pointing to the IMU or a magnetic environment rather than procedure.

would_settle_it.what: FWAP IMU and magnetometer check values at the failed preflight, to see which check tripped and whether the field looks disturbed
Repeat the preflight at a different site away from reinforced concrete to test the magnetic disturbance theory

reasoning: The only log review in the ticket says the warning came from the FWAP IMU error checks, and that IMU includes a magnetometer. Because the fault occurred across several aircraft and GCS units, an engineer suspected a local magnetic disturbance, but no test confirmed it. That narrows the failure to the FWAP IMU check, not to a part or a cause.
notes: The Root Cause field (wizard restart procedure) is not supported by any text in this ticket; it may have been carried over from VXEP-366 on the same aircraft. "Multiple AVs" were affected, so this is not one aircraft fault.

event: Aircraft 546 attempted to transition to VTOL for landing after a mission, lost about 350 to 420 ft in roughly 30 seconds, and crashed west of the landing zone; the aircraft was a total loss.
failure_mode: Rapid altitude loss during early VTOL landing while the VTOL AP was still in land state 2 (waiting for LZ proximity); cause unknown
contributing: VTOL SD card removed by the customer and lost, so no VTOL logs
VTOL AP board damaged and would not power up
Lift current about 20% lower than a reference landing with sustained high throttle
Forward motor held high throttle longer than typical during transition

evidence.quote: Summary So Far: Although a VTOL land abort was logged and initiated due to an attitude fault, the abort was most likely not the cause of the crash. While log message timestamps are not precise due to internal system latency, the abort likely occurred after, or during, the impact.

At the end of the XCOM data log the vehicle was in the state of waiting for proximity to the LZ. Neither the fixed wing autopilot nor the VTOL autopilot had advanced to the descension state. This means the vehicle should not have started descending.

Low Lift Power: Comparing data from an NCR flight indicates that during this landing the lift system consumed ~20% less current during landing than some SCO flight data. The current level is also sustained as is the sustained high throttle value.
@Pat Wells Don’t think there’s anything remaining from engineering to do then. The VTOL AP board is also damaged and will not power up.

team_view_in_comments: the abort was most likely not the cause of the crash

would_settle_it.what: The missing VTOL autopilot SD card from the 4/13 flight: VTOL logs for attitude, lift thrust and land state during the descent
XComm XCL00134 lift current, VTOL throttles and fault flags during the 30 seconds before impact

reasoning: XComm data show the vehicle lost altitude rapidly while neither autopilot had entered the descent state, with lower than typical lift current at sustained high throttle. The logged land abort and lift fault came after or during impact, and the 12V bus drop to the VTOL AP matches impact damage. Without VTOL logs the reason the aircraft descended cannot be identified, so the evidence does not get past the symptom.
notes: Customer report attributes the crash to "Climb abort, lift system fault"; the investigation found the abort followed impact. The AAR sent in January 2025 was from the 4/12 flight, not the incident flight. Resolution was Cannot Reproduce; goodwill replacement shipped under RMA-238.

event: On aircraft 426 during VTOL landing, the vehicle descended very slowly from altitude, drained the battery to about 12%, lost control near the ground and came to rest on a fence about 15 m from the landing site; no damage.
component: VTOL AP AGL altitude estimate (LRF range fusion and baro AGL offset)
failure_mode: Spurious LRF ranges taken during fixed-wing flight were fused into the AGL estimate, giving about a 200 ft offset, so the vehicle switched to the 3 ft/s slow descent about 200 ft too high
contributing: Degraded VTOL main battery with low starting charge
Position overshoot on transition in wind delayed the descent
Nudge commands moved the position setpoint over the fence

evidence.quote: This issue is resolved. The problem was identified and a software fix has been implemented. The laser range finder occasionally picks up spurious range measurements during fixed wing flight and  the VTOL INS incorporates this range data into its relative altitude estimates. The software has been updated to ignore any LRF range measurements made during fixed-wing flight.
- 200 ft offset error resulted in transition to 3 ft/s descent rate 200 ft higher above ground than intenede (compared to 7.5 ft/s before reaching ground level)
- Apparently degraded VTOL main battery put operators under additional pressure as AV neared the ground
This is a 2-line change to ensure that the baro agl offset is only calculated when in VTOL flight (i.e. not in fixed-wing when the vehicle is up and away).

team_root_cause: Spurious LRF measurements made during phases of flight in which they aren’t expected and used in INS estimates for AGL altitude. The AV then thinks it is much closer to the ground than it actually is. As a result, it enters the slow descent phase of VTOL landing too soon and a very slow descent from high altitude results. The battery on the vehicle appears somewhat degraded and the charge level was not high to begin with. The slow descent resulted in battery exaustion resulting in loss of attitude control near the fence on the ground.
reasoning: Log analysis found a 200 ft AGL offset that made the vehicle start the 3 ft/s final descent 200 ft too high, giving a long slow descent that exhausted a degraded battery. The offset came from spurious LRF ranges during fixed-wing flight being used in the AGL estimate. The fix to calculate the baro AGL offset only in VTOL flight reproduced the corruption in HIL and corrected it, with v426 listed among the field cases.
notes: FS2-1753 first described the cause as a barometric drop mismatch between baro AGL and LRF AGL; the final Root Cause and the FS2-1807 test work put it on spurious LRF updates corrupting the baro AGL offset. The FS2-1807 slides say the exact corruption mechanism is still future work.

event: About three minutes after launch on aircraft 439, the vehicle went into an automatic Low Energy RTB that the operator could not cancel, although the GCS showed 75% main battery and 70% HLB; the aircraft landed without damage.
component: Launch wizard battery model selection (default battery model loaded after a mid-wizard vehicle restart)
failure_mode: Vehicle was power cycled during the launch wizard and the wizard was not restarted, so the FWAP used a default battery model with much lower endurance and triggered a Low Energy RTB
contributing: Software silently falls back to a default battery model after reconnect
Operations manual had no caution to restart the wizard after a power cycle
XComm datalog missing from the AAR for the incident period

evidence.quote: On the last flight, during the pre-flight phase, the vehicle was restarted in the middle of the launch wizard. I believe this was probably to resolve a sensor calibration error. Once the vehicle reconnected the launch wizard was not restarted. Instead, the operator proceeded from the same page of the launch wizard.

This sequence results in the vehicle using an incorrect (default) battery model. The battery model is what the vehicle uses to calculate endurance. The battery model used by default has a severely reduced endurance. I’m guessing it’s a model of a really old battery that used to be used on a predecessor to the current VXE-30. This is the reason the vehicle activated a low battery RTB ~ 3 minutes into the flight.
I was able to recreate this issue in our HIL by following the same steps.
Awaiting shipment back to customer. No Fault found on this aircraft. No repairs or rework required.

team_root_cause: Launch wizard was not restarted after resetting the vehicle.
reasoning: The Low Energy RTB was traced in the FWAP code to RTB time versus battery endurance. The XComm event log shows the vehicle was reset during the launch wizard without restarting it, which leaves a default battery model with very low endurance, and the same steps reproduced the RTB on the HIL. The returned aircraft was found to have no fault.
notes: The roll fault in the logs is normal on VTOL transitions per engineering. Why the operator pause request was rejected was raised but not answered in the ticket. The customer link to "HLB errors" was later moved to VXEP-532. The RMA-247 induction PDF has no extracted text.

event: On fuel cell aircraft 523, the HLB kept discharging after launch on several flights and the aircraft reported failure to maintain altitude, so the operators landed early and paused flight operations.
failure_mode: Pitot zero calibrated with pressure applied, so indicated airspeed read low; the aircraft flew faster than commanded, used near dash power in cruise, and power demand exceeded fuel cell output, draining the HLB
contributing: Possible operator error applying pitot pressure during the shield step
Possible software delay between calibration command and application (tests found 0.5 to 1 s)
Launch wizard does not check calibration quality

evidence.quote: @Cameron Chapman apologies I had shared some IM’s with @Jason Scherer on the side but did not update this issue.  This looked to me like a bad airdata calibration.  The groundspeed is consistently well above the airspeed.  We saw something similar happen on AV477 (I linked that issue above also).  Unfortunately I don’t have TAS in the xcomm log and I don’t see a VTOL log with this, but unless it was an extremely hot day I suspect a bad airdata cal.

- 4/23/23: I charted the Throttle Vs Power curves from XCL00050 (original cruise motor) and XCL00052 (Spare cruise motor). The power draw is nearly the same. This tells us that the issue is not with the motor. I also charted throttle vs power curves from another vehicle. This standard vehicle is drawing nearly half the power as VXE-523 for the same throttle value. See slide number 8 and 9 here:  Vehicle Investigation VXEP-368 v523 Data for charts here: VXE-523 investigation data XCL00050.CSV

The fuel cell from V523’s AAR  seems to be working well.  I see good power output after takeoff with a reasonable stack voltage and fuel consumption.  I do not understand where the ‘reporting [of] battery current of “-10”’ is coming from in the vehicle software, but I do not see any indication of negative current in the fuel cell files.  I did see that the comparison of HLB voltage (as measured at the fuel cell) and the HLB state of charge seems to be very noisy, and perhaps scaled inaccurately?

@Pat Wells I got pulled into a few other tasks, but my investigation was leading me to believe that the air speed data was reporting lower than actual. I base this on the comparison with ground speed consistently higher, the motor throttle higher, the altitude is reported as commanded, and the vehicle is pitching down more significantly than normal. If the vehicle thinks it’s flying slow it will increase throttle to maintain the commanded altitude. But if it’s flying faster than it thinks, it will need to pitch down to maintain the same altitude.

For this particular bird, an updated air data calibration can be performed.  This will likely resolve the issue.  After the airdata cal is completed, pressure can be applied and the airspeed reading observed.  The sensor is expected to read above 60 knots for a good cal.  Both 477 and 523 read below 40 knots with pressure applied.

team_root_cause:
Pitot calibration errors caused the air vehicle to fly too fast, resulting in more thrust usage than typical.
Root cause of calibration errors is unclear.  Leading theory is operator error, software issue causing delay in calibration, or some combination of both.

would_settle_it.what: XComm event log timing of SEND AIRDATA CAL against the pitot pressure step, as done for AV477 in VXEP-292
Ground test after a fresh air data calibration to confirm airspeed reads above 60 knots with pressure applied

reasoning: The fuel cell output looked normal, and swapping the cruise motor did not change throttle versus power, so the fuel cell and forward motor were ruled out. Groundspeed was consistently above airspeed, with high throttle and nose-down pitch, which fits an airspeed reading too low after a bad pitot zero; the pitot check read below 40 knots against a 60 knot expectation. The resulting high cruise power exceeded fuel cell output and drained the HLB.
notes: The two CSV summaries hold only column lists and row counts (892 and 659 rows), no logger header lines. Why the calibration was bad (operator pressure during the shield step or software delay) was not settled here; the sister case VXEP-292 later concluded operator error as best guess. A Low Energy RTB applies in fuel cell configuration (VXEP-377).

event: On aircraft 541, fuel cell D4500638 showed an error during preflight and shut itself off in flight; after restarting it the error persisted and the aircraft landed early.
component: Fuel cell stack (cell and reactor holder), D450XR SN D4500638
failure_mode: Internal cell crack in the stack giving poor stack health and in-flight fuel cell shutdown
contributing: Suspected hard landings (known cause of cell and reactor holder cracking)
Return shipment in non-standard packaging may have added damage
Fuel calibration parameters found at default
Serial number misreported in the MCU (0639)

evidence.quote: Stack was found to be in poor health.
- Confirmed to be Cell Crack

Cell Cracking is a common source of system failure and can occur from a number of root causes. In this case, it is difficult to surmise exact cause as the unit was returned in improper shipping case, resulting in additional damage to the system. Replacement stack is requested.
Anode calibration seems valid, Fuel calibration parameters appear to be default.  V&I calibrations seem valid.

team_root_cause: Suspected internal cell crack. Due to shipping conditions, exact root cause is extremely difficult to assess. Stack failure due to cell & reactor holder cracking is known to be a common failure mode caused by hard landings and propagates over time.

would_settle_it.what: Condition of the returned unit and packaging, to judge how much damage happened in shipping
Photos and notes of the cracked cell and reactor holder location and fracture appearance

reasoning: Incoming QC at Ann Arbor found the stack in poor health, and the Plan records that dissection confirmed a cell crack; the stack was replaced and the unit passed validation. The cause of the crack is not established because the unit came back in improper packaging, so hard landings remain only the usual suspect.
notes: The Root Cause field says "suspected" while the Plan says "Confirmed to be Cell Crack"; I treat the crack as confirmed by dissection but give medium confidence because no dissection findings are in the export. RMA-242 lists vehicle tail 528 while this ticket says 541. The Incoming QC log (650 KB) was scanned for fault columns, stack current and voltage rather than read line by line; no fault flags were set. The DD1149 PDF has no extracted text.
